newsitem.title: USA: "Fed-watch" to keep Dow slightly lower at opening.
newsitem.headline: "Fed-watch" to keep Dow slightly lower at opening.

text.p: U.S. stocks are expected to open slightly lower this morning, as uncertainty about the future of interest rates drags on market sentiment despite Monday's record close.
Skittish investors are unlikely to take any strong positions until the Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) emerges from its meeting today with an announcement, analysts said.
The Dow rose six to about 5895, toppling the record it set last Monday of 5889.20.
"It should open unchanged to slightly lower, maybe a few points down, but then we could see a reversal," said Westfalia Investments research director Peter Cardillo.

"We're going to on hold as people concentrate on the Fed. A real negative would be a raise in rates by 50 basis points ... If they don't raise rates, the bond market will sell off, putting some pressure on stocks. The market has already discounted a 25 basis point hike in short term rates," he said.

"It looks a little lower," said Prudential market analyst Larry Wachtel of the opening. "This is going to be a hesitant session, and with the news coming maybe around 2:15 (EDT/1815 GMT), there will be a lot of watchful waiting.
"We should also sees some response to the consumer confidence numbers, which should fall," Wachtel said.
At 1000 EDT/1400 GMT, September consumer confidence is due. It is expected to fall to 107 from 109.4 in August.
AT&T Corp's warning that third and fourth quarter profits could be disappointing could also pull the Dow lower.
The long bond was up 1/32 to yield 7.02 percent.
Tokyo stocks ended mixed, with most participants on the sidelines awaiting the outcome of the U.S. policy meeting, with the Nikkei 225 closing up 60 to 21,172.
In London, the FTSE-100 index was off about 14 to 3906. U.S. stocks in London were steady to lightly firmer, buoyed by the Dow's rebound on Monday.
The dollar was also idling in Europe, awaiting the meeting.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column says short-sellers who bet on Chesapeake Energy have gotten the short end of the stick, and some are complaining that stockholder Fidelity Investments is using tactics to squeeze out the shorts. Fidelity says it doesn't engage in such tactics.
The New York Times Marketplace column says ARCO is heading to Russia to seek new oil reserves.
